passage: In the Toronto office kitchen, the sign-up sheet for the city marathon had eighteen names on it. "You're the only one on the team who hasn't signed," Yosef said, grinning, pen held out. Noa took the pen, then paused. She asked herself two questions she'd started using lately: Why do I want this? And would I still do it if nobody ever knew? The honest answers were: because everyone else is, and no. She hated long runs; she loved her Saturday swims. "Not this one," she said, handing the pen back. "But I'll be at the finish line with snacks and a very loud sign." Yosef laughed. "Deal." Two weeks later she signed up for the office's open-water swim, alone on the sheet, and didn't mind at all.

qa.q: How many names were on the marathon sign-up sheet?
qa.a: The sheet had eighteen names on it.

qa.q: What did Noa realise when she answered her two questions honestly?
qa.a: Noa felt relieved to admit she only wanted to sign because everyone else had, and that she'd never run it if nobody knew, since she hated long runs.

qa.q: How did Noa stay connected to the team while saying no?
qa.a: She offered to be at the finish line with snacks and a loud sign, backing them without running a race she didn't want.

qa.q: How does Yosef react to Noa's choice?
qa.a: Yosef laughs and says 'Deal', showing Yosef accepts her choice and her offer to cheer.

grounding: A young woman checks why she wants to join a popular marathon, declines, stays connected, and later picks a swim alone.

passage: At the agricultural research institute, the new drone-mapping project was the talk of the canteen. Nine of the twelve junior scientists had already asked to move onto it. "You're joining, right?" Kishore asked Gurleen, sliding into the chair opposite. Gurleen stirred her tea. She had a habit of asking herself, before any big move: Why do I want this? And what would I pick if nobody ever knew my choice? She thought about it that evening, sketching on the back of a lab report. The answer surprised her. She did want it; she'd been curious about soil mapping for years, long before it was fashionable. The next morning she applied, and wrote exactly which part she wanted to work on. "Following the herd?" Kishore teased. "Walking with it," she said. "On purpose."

qa.q: How many junior scientists had already asked to move onto the drone project?
qa.a: Nine of the twelve junior scientists had.

qa.q: Why was Gurleen surprised by her own answer?
qa.a: She half expected to find she was just following the crowd, but found she'd been curious about soil mapping for years and really wanted it.

qa.q: What did writing exactly which part she wanted add to Gurleen's application?
qa.a: It showed her choice came from her own interest and gave her a clear role, instead of just joining a crowd.

qa.q: What does Kishore's teasing 'Following the herd?' suggest Kishore assumed?
qa.a: Kishore seems to assume she's joining because everyone else did, not knowing she had checked her own reasons first.

grounding: A young scientist asks herself why she wants to join a popular project and joins it deliberately, for her own reasons.

passage:
Dear Hrithik,
You asked if I'm moving to Bengaluru like everyone else. Pankaj left in March, then Rupal, then half my college group. My phone is full of their new office photos. For a month I kept opening job sites at midnight.
Then I did what Mummy taught us: I asked myself why I wanted it. Honestly, mostly so I wouldn't feel left behind. Then I asked what I'd choose if none of them would ever find out. That one was easy. I'd stay in Indore, keep teaching at the school, and finish my B.Ed.
So I'm staying, on purpose this time, not because I'm scared to go. If one day I want Bengaluru for my own reasons, I'll go then.
Your didi,
Sunita

qa.q: What would Sunita choose if none of the friends would ever find out?
qa.a: She'd stay in Indore, keep teaching at the school, and finish her B.Ed.

qa.q: Why did Sunita keep opening job sites at midnight?
qa.a: With half her college group posting office photos, she felt left behind and anxious to keep up.

qa.q: What makes Sunita's decision deliberate rather than fearful?
qa.a: She checked both her reason for wanting to go and what she'd choose in private, and left the door open to go later for her own reasons.

qa.q: How might Hrithik feel reading Sunita didi's answer?
qa.a: Hrithik may feel reassured that she's staying by choice, and maybe pick up a way to make Hrithik's own decisions. 🙂

grounding: A young teacher asks why she wants to follow friends to a new city and what she'd pick privately, then stays on purpose.

passage:
Arohi, you asked why I'm not doing the MBA coaching everyone from our batch joined. I'm Hansa, and I'll be honest, I nearly did.
Twelve of our friends signed up in one week. The group chat was all mock test scores. I felt left behind, like the only girl still standing at the bus stop after the bus left. I had the form filled.
Then I asked myself two questions. Why do I want this? And if nobody ever knew whether I did an MBA, would I still choose it? The honest answer to the second one was no. I like my job at the textile cooperative. What I actually want is to learn design software, which the MBA wouldn't give me.
So I didn't join. I signed up for an evening design course instead. I still go to their mock-test parties with snacks. I'm with them, just not in the same boat.

qa.q: How many friends signed up for the MBA coaching in one week?
qa.a: Twelve of our friends signed up in one week.

qa.q: How did Hansa feel when her friends all joined, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt left behind, like the only girl still standing at the bus stop after the bus left, and had even filled in the form.

qa.q: Which two questions changed Hansa's decision, and what did she choose?
qa.a: She asked why she wanted it and whether she would choose it if nobody knew, and chose an evening design course instead of the MBA coaching.

qa.q: How might Arohi see Hansa's choice?
qa.a: Arohi might admire that Hansa stayed close to the group, bringing snacks to their parties, while making a decision based on what Hansa actually wants.

grounding: It shows a mature person asking why she wants something and what she would choose if nobody knew, then deliberately choosing not to follow the crowd.

passage:
I'm Leela, and I live one floor below Seema in our Goa housing society. In March, half the building started going to the Sunday beach cleanup. Photos everywhere, matching caps. Seema, twenty-five, didn't join at first. She told me, "I don't want to go just because it's the thing everyone's posting."
I noticed she went down to the beach alone one weekday evening and walked the whole stretch, looking at the plastic by the rocks. The next week she asked the organiser what happened to the waste after they bagged it. She also asked me, half joking, "Would I go if no one ever took a photo?"
I can't tell you what she decided inside. But the following Sunday she was there at seven, no cap, sorting bottles from wrappers by herself. When someone lifted a phone for a group photo, she smiled, waved, and kept sorting.

qa.q: What did Seema ask the organiser?
qa.a: She asked what happened to the waste after they bagged it.

qa.q: What does Seema's question, 'Would I go if no one ever took a photo?', suggest she wanted to know?
qa.a: It suggests she wanted to be sure she cared about the beach itself, not just about joining what everyone was posting.

qa.q: What did Seema do before joining, and why does that make the choice more her own?
qa.a: She walked the beach alone, asked where the waste went, and questioned her own reasons, so when she joined it was a deliberate choice.

qa.q: How does Leela see Seema's decision to join?
qa.a: Leela noticed the difference between Seema and the crowd, careful not to claim to know her mind, but seeing her work without a cap and keep sorting during the photo.

grounding: Told by a neighbour, it shows a mature person asking why she wants to join and whether she would if nobody knew, then joining the crowd deliberately.
